title: ST2 Example 6 — CT4 Style & Calculations
description: 100 marks: deployment capacity, queue growth, reliability and software metrics, plus diagram drawing, matching and scenarios.
scope: L17–L33 and L35 revision, including SOA (L26) and Microservices (L27)
reference: User-supplied actual CT4 assessment export; see ct4-style-analysis.md

questions.prompt: LabReserve’s team wants a booking application structured using Model–View–Controller. Draw the architecture on paper or in draw.io, then explain it. Keep your drawing for self-assessment; the text box can hold a description.

parts.prompt: 1. Draw and label Model, View and Controller, with labelled interaction directions. (5 marks)
parts.answer: One valid MVC sketch: User interacts with View; input is routed to Controller; Controller invokes Model operations; View renders Model state using the chosen MVC variant. Label the Controller’s selection/update of the View where applicable. MVC implementations differ in observation/rendering direction; award a coherent variant with separated responsibilities.
rubric: 3: correctly labelled components. 2: coherent labelled input/control/state/rendering interactions.

parts.prompt: 2. Explain each responsibility using the scenario, including where the no-double-booking rule belongs. (3 marks)
parts.answer: View displays laboratory availability and booking outcomes. Controller interprets reserve/cancel input and coordinates the operation. Model/domain service maintains booking state and enforces the no-overlap rule atomically on the server.
rubric: 1 each: three scenario-grounded responsibilities, with invariant enforcement in the model/domain.

questions.prompt: Match each software-quality metric with what it measures. Use each answer once.
options: Relatedness of responsibilities within a module

items.explanation: Each decision adds another independent control-flow route. This metric concerns paths through code; it does not count dependencies or establish correctness.

items.answer: Relatedness of responsibilities within a module
items.explanation: Responsibilities that contribute to one purpose belong together. Cohesion describes relationships inside a module, whereas coupling describes dependencies between modules.
A change to one module may affect another through their dependencies. Coupling therefore describes relationships across boundaries, rather than the focus of one module.
This combines several measures into a maintainability indicator. It is neither a raw defect count nor proof that a module is easy to change.

questions.prompt: LabReserve is preparing for peak registration. Use the original deployment/capacity diagram below. A student is active when they generate requests at the stated fixed cadence; they may have overlapping requests. All capacities are aggregate hard limits with perfect load balancing. Use the fluid steady-state approximation: resource throughput = concurrent slots / seconds held. One API slot is occupied for the entire request duration. Every API pod eagerly reserves its full primary pool; there is no external pooler. All non-primary pools are shared aggregate limits as shown. The enrol/booking duration already includes broker-confirm waiting. No other bottlenecks, retries or failures occur. The broker starts empty, has enough storage and applies no backpressure; consumers sustain their stated rate. The queue is not required to stay bounded until part 7. Calculate theoretical upper bounds, not operational targets with safety headroom. Show formulas, substitutions and units.

parts.prompt: 1. Counting only the web tier, how many active students can be served? (3 marks)
parts.answer: Web throughput = 720 requests/s. Each student produces 1/6 requests/s. Active students = 720 × 6 = 4,320. This is only a web-tier upper bound.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Multiply instance count by each instance’s sustainable request rate.
Each student emits one request every 6 seconds, so multiply web requests/s by 6.

parts.prompt: 2. What is the largest total API pod count allowed by primary connection reservations? (3 marks)
parts.answer: Usable connections = 150 − 30 = 120. Maximum pods = floor(120 / 15) = 8; the ninth would reserve 135 > 120.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Subtract reserved administrative connections from the primary connection limit.
Divide usable connections by the full reserved per-pod pool and floor to a whole pod.

parts.prompt: 3. At that pod count, what is the maximum booking throughput? Compare API slots, primary transactions, eligibility checks and broker confirms. Reads are absent for this part. (3 marks)
parts.answer: API slots = 240 / 0.600 = 400 bookings/s. Primary connections = 120 / 0.120 = 1000 transactions/s. Eligibility checks = 30 / 0.300 = 100/s. Confirms = 250/s. Web = 720/s. Minimum = 100 bookings/s, limited by eligibility checks. Database-only transaction capacity is not end-to-end capacity.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Divide all API request slots by total write-request occupancy in seconds.
Divide usable primary connections by transaction hold time in seconds.
Divide check-service concurrency by one check’s duration in seconds.
The diagram gives this aggregate confirmation limit directly.
Take the smallest end-to-end bound, including the web tier.
The external check bound is lower than the API, primary, web and confirmation bounds.

parts.prompt: 4. What is the replica read throughput bound, and the corresponding total request bound under the stated read/write mix? (3 marks)
parts.answer: 40 / 0.080 = 500 reads/s. Because reads are 80% of requests, total request bound = 500 / 0.80 = 625 requests/s.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Use replica connection hold time, not the complete read duration.
Divide the read rate by the read fraction because only that fraction of total traffic uses this path.

parts.prompt: 5. Across the complete synchronous request path at the part-2 pod count, how many active students can be supported? Compare the web, API, read, write/check and confirm limits. (3 marks)
parts.answer: Mean API occupancy = 0.8 × 0.1 + 0.2 × 0.6 = 0.2 s/request; API bound = 240 / 0.2 = 1200.00 total requests/s. Other total-request bounds: web 720; replica 625; primary 5000; eligibility 500; broker confirms 1250. Minimum = 500 requests/s. Active students = 500 × 6 = 3,000. Eligibility is the bottleneck; bookings occur at 100/s.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Weight each full request duration by its share of traffic.
Divide all API slots by weighted occupancy; two decimal places are sufficient.
The smallest mix-adjusted total bound is 500 requests/s; multiply by the 6-second cadence.
Compare every limit in total requests/s, rather than comparing a read rate directly with a write rate.

parts.prompt: 6. At the part-5 load, how many email messages are waiting after 15 minutes? Start with an empty broker. (3 marks)
parts.answer: Arrival rate = 500 × 0.2 = 100 messages/s. Net queue growth = 100 − 70 = 30 messages/s. Elapsed time = 15 × 60 = 900 seconds. Waiting messages = max(0, 30 × 900) = 27,000. Consumer throughput is distinct from broker-confirm throughput.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Multiply completed total requests/s by the write fraction; each write emits one message.
Subtract 70 consumer messages/s, then multiply net growth by 900 seconds.

parts.prompt: 7. What is the largest active-student load for which the email queue does not grow indefinitely? (3 marks)
parts.answer: For a bounded queue in this deterministic model, message arrival must be ≤ 70/s. Total request bound = 70 / 0.2 = 350/s. Other bounds are higher. Active students ≤ 350 × 6 = 2,100. Equality is the theoretical limit; real variable workloads need spare capacity.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: For a bounded queue, sustained arrivals cannot exceed sustained consumer processing.
Divide the publication/consumer rate by the write fraction.
Multiply queue-stable total rate by cadence and verify that other resource bounds are higher.

parts.prompt: 8. Double eligibility-check concurrency to 60, retaining every other limit. Calculate the new supported student count and identify the new limiting resource. (3 marks)
parts.answer: Eligibility capacity becomes 60 / 0.300 = 200 bookings/s, permitting 1,000 total requests/s. Reads remain capped at 40 / 0.080 = 500/s, permitting 500 / 0.80 = 625 total requests/s. Web permits 720/s and API slots permit 240 / 0.20 = 1,200 total requests/s. New capacity = 625 × 6 = 3,750 active students, limited by read-replica connections.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.prompt: Active students after the proposed change
checks.explanation: Recompute the changed resource and take the minimum of all unchanged and changed bounds.
After the change, the replica allows only 625 total requests/s.

questions.prompt: Match each isolation-stack element with its defining role. Use each answer once.
options: Execution flow within a process sharing its address space
Process isolation and resource controls using the host kernel
Layer creating and managing virtual machines
Hardware providing processor, memory and devices

items.answer: Hardware providing processor, memory and devices
items.explanation: The host is the actual machine supplying CPU, memory and devices. Virtual machines and containers consume these resources through software layers.

items.answer: Layer creating and managing virtual machines
items.explanation: A hypervisor provides virtual hardware and manages guest virtual machines. It differs from container isolation, which normally shares the host kernel.

items.answer: Process isolation and resource controls using the host kernel
items.explanation: Namespaces, resource controls and related restrictions isolate processes while they use the host kernel. A container does not normally contain a separate booted guest kernel.

items.answer: Execution flow within a process sharing its address space
items.explanation: Threads are execution flows within a process and share that process’s address space. They are not independent machines or container runtimes.

questions.prompt: A module has length 25, fan-in 4 and fan-out 3. Its application contains 24 confirmed defects in 8 KLOC. A separate single-entry, single-exit function has four binary decisions: two loops and two if-statements (no compound Boolean predicates). Use information-flow complexity = length × (fan-in × fan-out)^2; defect density = defects / KLOC; cyclomatic complexity = binary decisions + 1.

parts.prompt: 1. Calculate original information-flow complexity. (2 marks)
parts.answer: 25 × (4 × 3)² = 25 × 144 = 3,600. Square the product of fan-in and fan-out.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 2. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Multiply length by the square of fan-in × fan-out; do not square length.

parts.prompt: 2. Fan-out is reduced to 1, with length and fan-in unchanged. Calculate the new score and percentage reduction. Explain one limit of this result. (2 marks)
parts.answer: New score = 25 × (4 × 1)² = 400. Reduction = (3600 − 400) / 3600 × 100% = 88.89%. This predictor alone does not prove correctness or maintainability; functional checks and contextual review remain necessary.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 1.5. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.
Self-assessed reasoning: 0.5 marks. Explain why the metric does not prove correctness/maintainability.

checks.explanation: Keep length and fan-in unchanged; substitute the new fan-out.
Use (old − new) / old × 100; round to two decimals.

parts.prompt: 3. Calculate defect density and give the unit. (2 marks)
parts.answer: 24 / 8 = 3 defects/KLOC. The KLOC denominator is already in thousands of lines; do not divide the result by another thousand.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 2. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Divide defect count by size already expressed in KLOC; do not divide again by 1,000.

parts.prompt: 4. Calculate cyclomatic complexity and state what it counts. (2 marks)
parts.answer: 4 + 1 = 5. It counts linearly independent control-flow paths under the stated simplified binary-decision model; it is different from information-flow complexity.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 1. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.
Self-assessed reasoning: 1 marks. Explain that cyclomatic complexity counts independent control-flow paths.

checks.explanation: Under the stated binary-decision model, add one to the decision count.

questions.prompt: Traffic jumps from 40 to 900 requests/s in two seconds, then immediately falls. The team wants to observe the system’s response to abrupt load change. What is the most specific testing category?
questions.explanation: The defining feature is an abrupt burst and drop. Stress testing instead emphasises exceeding sustainable limits and overload/recovery.
optionExplanations: The abrupt rise and fall identifies spike testing.
Soak testing maintains load for a long period to expose accumulation.
A unit test targets an isolated unit and is not defined by a sudden traffic burst.
Code review is inspection, rather than executing a workload change.

questions.prompt: Match each term with its precise meaning. Use each answer once.
options: Verifies the interface behaviour that a consumer depends on
Repeated execution has the same intended effect as one execution
Number of other components called by a component
Number of other components calling a component

items.answer: Number of other components calling a component
items.explanation: Count incoming component dependencies: how many other components call this one. High fan-in can indicate reuse and also a large impact if this component changes.

items.answer: Number of other components called by a component
items.explanation: Count outgoing component dependencies: how many other components this one calls. Many outgoing dependencies can increase coordination and change complexity.

items.answer: Repeated execution has the same intended effect as one execution
items.explanation: Repeating an operation preserves the intended business effect of executing it once. This helps handle retries and duplicate delivery; it does not require that the operation run only once.

items.answer: Verifies the interface behaviour that a consumer depends on
items.explanation: The check captures the response/interface behaviour that a consumer actually needs. It can detect incompatible provider changes that unit tests inside either service miss.

questions.prompt: LabReserve exposes a file-search API. A user supplies a search term which is inserted directly into a SQL string. Select all appropriate responses. The stated practice negative-marking rule applies.
options: Use parameterised queries for data values.
Treat client-side validation as the security boundary.
Run the database account with only necessary permissions.
Disable all audit logs to avoid leaking search data.
Add authorised injection tests in a controlled test environment.
Review generated query-building code before merging.
questions.explanation: Parameter binding separates data from SQL structure. Least privilege, authorised tests and code review address exposure and regression. Client validation is bypassable; logs should be designed to limit sensitive content rather than universally disabled.
optionExplanations: Parameter binding treats the search term as data instead of concatenated SQL structure.
Client validation can be bypassed; server-side controls remain necessary.
Restricting database privileges limits damage if an injection or other compromise occurs.
Disabling all logs removes evidence; design safe useful logs without recording sensitive search data unnecessarily.
Controlled authorised injection tests verify how the real boundary handles malicious inputs.
Generated code may recreate unsafe string concatenation and remains the team’s review responsibility.

questions.prompt: During a LabReserve demo, the presenter claims “99.9% availability” from one successful run, opens an unexplained administrator-only screen, and spends the last minute repeatedly refreshing a failed external eligibility request. Identify three distinct problems. For each, explain its effect on assessment and give one concrete correction.

parts.prompt: Give three problem/effect/correction triples. (6 marks)
parts.answer: 1. Unsupported availability claim confuses a demonstration with sustained evidence: present an observed failure/repair record and clearly stated measurement window. 2. An unexplained admin-only screen hides user intent and role behaviour: introduce a student task and demonstrate representative role permissions. 3. Repeated refreshes consume evidence time and obscure dependency failure handling: time-box recovery, show honest pending/error state, and use a disclosed fallback or recording with its limitations.
rubric: 2 each for three distinct triples: 0.5 problem, 0.5 effect, 1 concrete correction.

questions.prompt: Match each reliability term to the course definition. Use each answer once.

items.explanation: Sum operating intervals and divide by observed failures. Repair intervals are excluded from the operating-time numerator.
Sum restoration intervals and divide by completed restorations. It measures recovery duration, rather than time spent operating successfully.
For this course, MTBF includes the mean operating interval and mean repair interval: MTTF + MTTR. Do not substitute it directly for uptime in the availability numerator.

questions.prompt: A compute service completes three operating/failure/repair cycles. It runs for 7.5 days, then takes 3 hours to restore; runs for 2 weeks, then takes 9 hours to restore; and runs for 204 hours, then takes 6 hours to restore. Observation stops when the third restoration completes. All downtime is counted in the repair intervals. Use the course convention MTBF = MTTF + MTTR and Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) × 100%. Show working. Round percentages to two decimal places; keep full precision in intermediate calculations.

parts.prompt: 1. Calculate MTTF and MTTR in hours. (4 marks)
parts.answer: 7.5 days × 24 = 180 h; 2 weeks × 7 × 24 = 336 h. Total operating time = 180 + 336 + 204 = 720 h; MTTF = 720 / 3 = 240 h. Repair time = 3 + 9 + 6 = 18 h; MTTR = 18 / 3 = 6 h.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 4. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Convert operating intervals to hours, sum them and divide by three failures.
Sum restoration durations only and divide by three restorations.

parts.prompt: 2. Calculate MTBF and availability. (3 marks)
parts.answer: MTBF = 240 + 6 = 246 h. Availability = 240 / 246 × 100% = 97.56%. This agrees with total uptime / total observed cycle time.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Use the stated course convention: MTTF + MTTR.
Divide mean uptime by mean uptime plus mean repair time, then multiply by 100; two decimal places.

parts.prompt: 3. Recovery automation changes MTTR to 1.5 hours while MTTF stays unchanged. Calculate availability and state whether fewer failures have been demonstrated. (3 marks)
parts.answer: Availability = 240 / (240 + 1.5) × 100% = 99.38%. Fewer failures have not been demonstrated: mean operating time is unchanged; restoration is faster. Availability improves through reduced downtime.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 2. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.
Self-assessed reasoning: 1 marks. Explain that faster restoration improves availability without demonstrating fewer failures.

checks.explanation: Keep MTTF at 240 h; substitute the faster MTTR in the denominator; two decimal places.

parts.prompt: 4. With the original MTTF, what is the maximum MTTR meeting availability ≥ 99.9%? Give hours to four decimal places and approximate minutes. Treat the unrounded value as the acceptance limit. (2 marks)
parts.answer: 240 / (240 + r) ≥ 0.999; hence r ≤ 240 × (1 / 0.999 − 1) = 0.2402 h ≈ 14.41 minutes. The exact unrounded expression is the limit; a rounded-up repair target could narrowly fail it.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 2. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Rearrange A = 240 / (240 + r): r ≤ 240 × (1/A − 1). Enter four decimal places.
Multiply the unrounded hour limit by 60; two decimal places.

questions.prompt: Match each code-quality practice with its most direct outcome. Use each answer once.
options: Records non-obvious reasons for design decisions
Keeps a component focused on one reason to change
Communicates the purpose of variables and operations

items.answer: Communicates the purpose of variables and operations
items.explanation: A useful name reveals intent and reduces the amount of surrounding code a reader must inspect. It helps comprehension but does not replace tests.

items.answer: Keeps a component focused on one reason to change
items.explanation: Responsibilities that change for different reasons are separated. This limits unrelated change impact and makes focused testing and maintenance easier.
Validate assumptions and handle unexpected inputs or states deliberately so they do not become uncontrolled failures. Silently ignoring every error is not defensive behaviour.

items.answer: Records non-obvious reasons for design decisions
items.explanation: Code often shows what happens, but not why a trade-off was chosen. A rationale comment records the reason rather than repeating an obvious statement.

questions.prompt: Read this self-contained UML deployment model. Boxes show device nodes, contained execution environments and deployed artifacts; connecting lines are communication paths. In text, the browser communicates with the API host over HTTPS/TLS 1.3, and the API host communicates with the database host over PostgreSQL wire protocol/TCP 5432. Answer from the labels rather than guessing a technology.

parts.prompt: 1. Is this a coherent deployment model? Give one diagram-based reason. (2 marks)
parts.answer: Yes. It shows artifacts located in execution environments on device nodes and labelled communication paths between deployed nodes. Naming a technology alone would not establish the deployment placement.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 1. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.
Self-assessed reasoning: 1 marks. Justify deployment validity from artifact placement and communication paths.

checks.explanation: The model places artifacts inside execution environments on devices and labels communication paths.

parts.prompt: 2. Identify the backend technology and database schema. (2 marks)
parts.answer: Backend: Python. Main schema: Bookings. PostgreSQL is the database engine, not the schema name.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 2. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Read the backend runtime/technology label on the API host.
The named schema is separate from PostgreSQL, which is the database engine.

parts.prompt: 3. Classify booking.py and identify the environment hosting it. (2 marks)
parts.answer: booking.py is a deployed artifact hosted in the Python runtime on the API host.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 2. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: The file is deployed executable/software content, rather than a physical machine or runtime.
The deployed file sits in the named runtime within the API host.

parts.prompt: 4. Name the database communication protocol/port, and explain why drawing only the software classes would not answer a deployment question. (2 marks)
parts.answer: PostgreSQL wire protocol over TCP port 5432. A class diagram shows software types and relationships; a deployment diagram additionally locates runtime artifacts on execution environments/devices and shows communication paths.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 1. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

questions.prompt: LabReserve’s team implements booking with a low-code workflow and a generated Python adapter to an eligibility service. A booking is committed locally before the adapter times out; retrying with a new request ID can create another booking. A new API release removes a status field used by the UI. Controls are visually inconsistent, and pending requests show “confirmed”. The team proposes a shared database for all future microservices, accessed directly by every service.

parts.prompt: 1. Give one design-system change and one user-feedback change, explaining their benefits. (2 marks)
parts.answer: Use a shared accessible booking/status component with consistent interaction and validation rules. Show accepted/pending until completion is known, then confirmed/failed with recovery guidance; this makes the displayed state truthful and reduces blind retries.
rubric: 1: shared design-system practice with benefit. 1: truthful state/feedback change with benefit.

parts.prompt: 2. Propose three CI/DevSecOps checks tied to this scenario. (3 marks)
parts.answer: Add a consumer contract compatibility check for the status field, an integration/fault-injection test for timeout/retry using a stable booking ID, and security/dependency/static checks plus manual review of the generated adapter and platform permissions. Evaluate the real boundary, not only a mocked success.
rubric: 1 each: three distinct scenario-linked checks with purpose.

parts.prompt: 3. Explain one cost of the shared-database proposal and recommend a service/contract boundary. (2 marks)
parts.answer: Direct cross-service table access couples schema changes and bypasses ownership/invariants, undermining independent releases. Let the booking owner enforce its data rules through a versioned API/event contract; other services call that boundary. This introduces network/consistency costs that need explicit handling.
rubric: 1: causal coupling/ownership cost. 1: appropriate owner boundary and contract.

parts.prompt: 4. State one domain invariant and one mitigation for low-code/generated-code risk. (2 marks)
parts.answer: Invariant: a resource/time slot must not have overlapping successful bookings; enforce uniqueness/transactions and preserve a stable idempotency key for repeated requests. Review and test workflow permissions, timeout/retry and exported/generated code; assign ownership and retain a rollback/migration path for platform constraints.
rubric: 1: grounded invariant with enforcement. 1: concrete platform/generated-code risk mitigation.
